about: A 15-credit Term 1 module for first-year BSc Politics and International Relations students that uses political philosophy to examine unequal power in modern life, including state power over citizens, employer power over workers, gender and racial hierarchies and North-South relations. It begins with contemporary theories of freedom and moves to coercion and consent, legitimacy and democracy, domination and oppression, justice, property and poverty, then reads canonical thinkers (Hobbes, Rousseau, Marx, Hayek) and less-studied ones (Macaulay, de Gouges, Douglass, Cooper, Nkrumah, Davis and the Combahee River Collective). The 2026/27 catalogue lists assessment as 100% coursework across two assessments.
topics: Inequalities of power in modern politics
Overlooked voices: Macaulay, de Gouges, Douglass, Cooper, Nkrumah, Davis and the Combahee River Collective

notes.h: Inequalities of power in modern politics
notes.body:
Political philosophy asks normative questions: how should power be distributed, and when is it justified? This module begins from the observation that modern life is marked by unequal power in many relationships: between states and citizens, employers and workers, men and women, racial groups, and rich and poor countries. Political theory helps us describe these inequalities, judge when they are unjust and think about remedies.

State and citizen
Max Weber's definition of the state as holding a monopoly of legitimate force (1919) shows that state power is a distinctive kind of power: it is backed by coercion and claims authority over everyone in a territory. Political philosophy asks what could justify it, a question taken up in later topics on coercion, consent and legitimacy.

Employer and worker
Elizabeth Anderson (Private Government, 2017) argues that many workplaces are governed like small authoritarian states: employers can set rules, monitor and discipline workers, sometimes including conduct outside work, with little accountability. She uses this to challenge the picture of employment as a purely voluntary exchange between equals. Defenders of the market reply that workers can quit, and that the employment contract is freely entered.

Gender
Carole Pateman (The Sexual Contract, 1988) argued that the classical social contract tradition presupposed an earlier sexual contract that subordinated women. Susan Moller Okin (Justice, Gender and the Family, 1989) argued that theories of justice neglect the family, a place where power and resources are unequally distributed.

Race
Charles Mills (The Racial Contract, 1997) argued that the social contract was also a racial contract that treated non-white people as less than full persons, so mainstream theory has idealised away real structures of white supremacy. W. E. B. Du Bois earlier analysed the colour line as the central problem of the twentieth century.

Global North and South
Frantz Fanon (The Wretched of the Earth, 1961) and Kwame Nkrumah (Neo-Colonialism, 1965) examined how colonial domination persisted after formal independence. Thomas Pogge (World Poverty and Human Rights, 2002) argued that the global institutional order imposed by rich states contributes to severe poverty. Edward Said (Orientalism, 1978) analysed how Western representations of the "Orient" supported domination.

Structural power and intersection
Iris Marion Young treated oppression as structural in Justice and the Politics of Difference (1990) and developed the idea of structural injustice in Responsibility for Justice (2011): injustice produced by the cumulative effect of many people following accepted rules, without a single dominator. Kimberle Crenshaw (1989) coined intersectionality to describe how overlapping systems of discrimination, such as race and sex, create distinct disadvantage which single-axis analysis misses. The Combahee River Collective (1977) had already analysed interlocking oppressions.

Methods in political philosophy
Philosophers analyse concepts (what is freedom?), test principles against cases and thought experiments, and examine arguments for consistency. They also ask which social facts matter: normative claims depend on how power actually works.

Exam tips: for each relationship, name the author, state the claim, and consider one objection; do not treat inequality as injustice without argument; show you understand the difference between description and evaluation.

Freedom is one of the central values of modern politics, but it has been understood in different ways. Debates about what freedom is shape arguments about what the state may do and what counts as oppression.

Negative and positive liberty
Isaiah Berlin's lecture "Two Concepts of Liberty" (1958; reprinted in Four Essays on Liberty, 1969) distinguished:
- Negative liberty: the absence of interference by others within the area in which a person could otherwise act. It answers the question "What is the area within which the subject — a person or group of persons — is or should be left to do or be what he is able to do or be, without interference by other persons?"
- Positive liberty: being one's own master, acting according to one's own will and rational purposes. It answers the question "Who governs me?", whereas negative liberty answers "How far does government interfere with me?"

Berlin favoured negative liberty and feared that positive liberty could be distorted. If the "real" self is identified with reason or the collective, rulers might claim to force people to be free by coercing their "lower" selves, a charge sometimes made against Rousseau (Social Contract, 1762: those who refuse the general will will be "forced to be free"). Critics say Berlin overstates the danger, that positive liberty includes autonomy as a respectable ideal, and that Berlin's own negative liberty needs to say which interferences count.

Gerald MacCallum (1967) argued that freedom is a triadic relation: an agent is free from some constraint to do or become something. Thus negative and positive freedom stress different parts of the same relation.

Hobbes and the "pure" negative view
Thomas Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651, ch. 21) defined liberty as the absence of external impediments to motion. Ian Carter (A Measure of Freedom, 1999) and Matthew Kramer (The Quality of Freedom, 2003) developed non-moralised accounts in which freedom depends on the physical obstacles in a person's way, not on whether those obstacles are justified.

Republican freedom: non-domination
Philip Pettit (Republicanism, 1997) and Quentin Skinner (Liberty before Liberalism, 1998) revived a republican, or neo-Roman, conception: freedom is not being subject to the arbitrary power of another. A person is unfree if someone has the capacity to interfere arbitrarily in their choices, even if the power is never used. The classic example is a slave with a kind master: no actual interference occurs, yet the slave is dependent on the master's goodwill and so unfree. Non-arbitrary interference, such as that of laws that track citizens' common interests, does not reduce freedom. This has implications for workplaces, the household and relations between citizens and officials.

Capability and freedom as opportunity
Amartya Sen (Development as Freedom, 1999) and Martha Nussbaum stress capabilities, what people are actually able to do and be. Rawls speaks of the "worth" of liberty, which depends on resources. These views argue that formal freedoms are valueless without material means.

Freedom and the market
Friedrich Hayek (The Constitution of Liberty, 1960) defined freedom as the absence of coercion by the arbitrary will of another. Poverty may be unfortunate but not an unfreedom. G. A. Cohen replied that capitalism restricts the freedom of workers who must sell their labour.

Mill and the harm principle
John Stuart Mill (On Liberty, 1859) argued that the only purpose for which power can rightfully be exercised over a member of a civilised community against his will is to prevent harm to others. This is a principle about the limits of social and legal interference.

Exam tips: define the concept used before applying it; show how the same case (a kind master, a poor person unable to afford a hospital) is judged differently under each conception.

The state claims authority over its citizens and enforces it with coercion. Political philosophy asks: what is coercion, when is consent meaningful, and what makes political power legitimate, meaning morally justified so that subjects have a duty to obey?

Power, authority and legitimacy
Power is the ability to get others to do things. Authority is the right to rule and to be obeyed. Legitimacy concerns whether the exercise of power is morally justified. Weber used legitimacy descriptively (people believe in it), while philosophers usually use it normatively (it is justified whether or not people believe it).

Coercion
Robert Nozick (1969) analysed coercion as a threat that makes a person worse off than their baseline if they refuse, whereas an offer makes a person better off. Alan Wertheimer (Coercion, 1987) argued that what counts as the baseline is itself a moral question. These definitions matter for deciding whether a choice is voluntary: for example, G. A. Cohen (1983) argued that workers who must sell their labour to survive are unfree collectively, even if each is free to choose among employers.

Consent theories
- Thomas Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651) argued that covenants made out of fear in the state of nature are still binding (ch. 14), so subjects may be obliged even if they submit because of fear of a conqueror.
- John Locke (Second Treatise, 1689) argued that legitimate government rests on consent, which can be express or tacit: by enjoying the benefits of the state, such as travelling on its highways, one consents tacitly (section 119). He argued that the majority may bind the minority once a community is formed.
- David Hume ("Of the Original Contract", 1748) objected that nobody has actually consented. He said that a person living in a country is like one carried on board a ship while asleep, who "consents" to the captain's rule by not jumping overboard. Realistically most people cannot leave.
- A. John Simmons (1979) and Robert Paul Wolff (In Defense of Anarchism, 1970) used these difficulties to defend philosophical anarchism: no state has a general authority over its subjects, though some of its commands may be justified for other reasons.

Alternatives to actual consent
- Hypothetical consent: Rawls (A Theory of Justice, 1971) asks what principles people would choose in an imagined original position. Critics (Dworkin) say that a hypothetical contract is not binding like a real one.
- Fairness: H. L. A. Hart (1955) argued that people who benefit from a cooperative scheme have a duty to do their share. Nozick replied that unrequested benefits do not create obligations.
- Natural duty: Rawls argued for a duty to support just institutions.
- Service conception: Joseph Raz (The Morality of Freedom, 1986) argued that authority is legitimate when subjects would better comply with reasons that apply to them by following its directives than by trying to act on those reasons themselves (the normal justification thesis).
- Public reason: Rawls (Political Liberalism, 1993) proposed the liberal principle of legitimacy: political power is justified when exercised in accordance with a constitution whose essentials all citizens, as free and equal, can endorse in the light of reasons they could reasonably accept. David Estlund (Democratic Authority, 2008) defends democratic authority by its epistemic qualities.

Exam tips: do not treat consent as one idea; identify whether the theory requires actual, tacit or hypothetical consent and give the main objection.

This topic asks how democracy relates to freedom and to the structures of domination and oppression. Does democracy protect against domination, or can majorities dominate minorities? What does it mean to be oppressed, and can it occur without an oppressor?

Democracy and non-domination
Philip Pettit (On the People's Terms, 2012) argues that a republican democracy should enable citizens to exercise control over government so that its power is not arbitrary. Elections are not enough: citizens also need effective means of contestation, such as courts, ombudsmen and the right to challenge decisions. Pettit calls this a contestatory conception of democracy. Domination by the majority is a real risk: Alexis de Tocqueville (1835) warned of the tyranny of the majority, and James Madison (Federalist No. 10, 1787) of factions. Constitutional rights, separation of powers and representation are institutional answers.

Domination at work and at home
Elizabeth Anderson (Private Government, 2017) and republican labour theorists argue that employees are dominated when employers have extensive power with little accountability. Carole Pateman (Participation and Democratic Theory, 1970) argued that democracy should extend to the workplace. Robert Dahl (A Preface to Economic Democracy, 1985) made similar arguments about firms. Feminists note that the household has long been treated as private and so outside justice.

Oppression
Marilyn Frye (The Politics of Reality, 1983) described oppression as a structure of forces that restrain and immobilise people, like the wires of a birdcage; looking at one wire does not explain why the bird is trapped. Iris Marion Young (1990) listed five faces of oppression:
- Exploitation: the transfer of the results of one group's labour to benefit another.
- Marginalisation: exclusion from useful participation in social life.
- Powerlessness: lacking authority or respect, as workers who take orders without making decisions.
- Cultural imperialism: the dominant group's experience and culture are made the norm, while the group is marked as different.
- Violence: systematic vulnerability to attack because of group membership.
For Young, oppression is structural and does not require tyrants. Social groups are important, and politics should recognise group differences.

Epistemic injustice
Miranda Fricker (Epistemic Injustice, 2007) distinguished testimonial injustice, where prejudice leads a hearer to give a speaker less credibility, and hermeneutical injustice, where a gap in shared interpretive resources puts someone at a disadvantage in making sense of their own experience (as before the concept of sexual harassment existed). This shows that oppression can operate in who is believed and which concepts are available.

Democratic inclusion
If oppressed groups are excluded from deliberation, democracy may reproduce domination. Young argued for group representation and communicative democracy. Critics argue that group rights risk fixing identities. Elizabeth Anderson (The Imperative of Integration, 2010) argued that democracy requires integration across social groups to remove segregation.

Exam tips: define domination and oppression precisely and give a case; show how democracy can both reduce and sustain domination.

What distribution of income, wealth and opportunity is just? This topic covers major theories of distributive justice and the moral questions raised by property and poverty.

Rawls: justice as fairness
John Rawls (A Theory of Justice, 1971) asks what principles free and equal persons would choose in the original position, behind a veil of ignorance that hides their class, talents, race, sex and conception of the good. Rawls argued they would choose two principles:
1. Equal basic liberties for all, with priority over the second principle.
2. Social and economic inequalities must (a) attach to positions open to all under fair equality of opportunity, and (b) be to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged (the difference principle).
The thought is that, since natural talents and social starting points are morally arbitrary, inequalities are justified only if they work for everyone, especially the worst off. In later work (notably Justice as Fairness: A Restatement, 2001) Rawls favoured a property-owning democracy or liberal socialism over welfare-state capitalism. He rejected utilitarianism because it does not take seriously the separateness of persons.

Nozick: entitlement
Robert Nozick (Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974) argued that a distribution is just if it arises from just steps. His entitlement theory has three principles: justice in acquisition (how unowned things can be acquired), justice in transfer (voluntary exchange or gift) and rectification of past injustice. Justice is historical, not patterned. In the Wilt Chamberlain example, people freely pay to watch a famous basketball player, and he ends up wealthy; if the initial distribution was just, so is the new one, so keeping a pattern would need continuous interference with liberty. Nozick wrote that taxation of earnings from labour is on a par with forced labour. Critics (G. A. Cohen, Self-Ownership, Freedom, and Equality, 1995) deny that self-ownership supports unrestricted property rights, and question the justice of initial appropriation.

Property
John Locke (Second Treatise, 1689) argued that people acquire property by mixing their labour with unowned things, provided there is "enough, and as good" left for others and nothing spoils. Marxists see property relations as the basis of class. Libertarians treat private property as central to liberty, while egalitarians argue that property rights are conventions that must be justified by their effects on all.

Luck egalitarianism and relational equality
Ronald Dworkin (1981, "What is Equality?") argued for equality of resources, in which people are responsible for their choices but not for their circumstances. Richard Arneson and G. A. Cohen (1989) developed this as luck egalitarianism: inequalities due to brute bad luck are unjust, while those due to choices are not. Elizabeth Anderson (1999, "What is the Point of Equality?") objected that this view is demeaning to those it labels as having been careless, and that equality is about social relations among equals, not the cancelling of luck. Amartya Sen (1979) asked "Equality of what?" and proposed capabilities. Harry Frankfurt (1987) argued that what matters morally is sufficiency, that everyone has enough, not equality.

Poverty and global justice
Peter Singer (1972, "Famine, Affluence and Morality") argued that if we can prevent something very bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance we ought to do so, which implies large duties to aid. Thomas Pogge (2002) argued that the global order harms the poor and creates negative duties. Rawls (The Law of Peoples, 1999) proposed a more limited duty of assistance to burdened societies and rejected a global difference principle. Philippe Van Parijs (Real Freedom for All, 1995) defended an unconditional basic income.

Exam tips: state the principle exactly, show how it applies to a case (an inheritance, a tax), and give the strongest objection to each theory.

Thomas Hobbes and Jean-Jacques Rousseau both use the idea of a state of nature and a social contract, yet reach very different conclusions about authority and freedom.

Hobbes: Leviathan (1651)
Writing after the English Civil War, Hobbes starts from a materialist view of human beings as self-preserving, with a natural right (jus naturale) to do what is necessary to preserve themselves. In the state of nature, with no common power, individuals are roughly equal in their capacity to kill one another. Hobbes identifies three causes of quarrel: competition, diffidence (fear and distrust) and glory. The result is a war of all against all, in which life is "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short" (ch. 13), with no industry, no arts and no society. Reason offers laws of nature that recommend seeking peace, but without enforcement, keeping promises is irrational for the first to comply.

The solution is a covenant in which each person authorises a sovereign, a man or assembly, to act on behalf of all and transfers the right of self-government to him. The sovereign has absolute authority and cannot be justly resisted, since the subjects are the authors of its acts and there is no higher judge. Obligation lasts as long as the sovereign can protect. One right cannot be given up: self-preservation, so subjects need not obey an order to kill themselves. Liberty for Hobbes is the silence of the law and absence of external impediments (ch. 21), a negative conception. Hobbes also argues that the sovereign should control doctrine, since conflicting opinions cause civil war. Critics say that Hobbes's solution produces a worse danger (the state) and that his state of nature is unrealistic about human psychology.

Rousseau: Discourse on Inequality (1755) and The Social Contract (1762)
Rousseau argued that Hobbes projected the vices of civilised society onto natural humanity. For Rousseau, humans in nature are driven by self-preservation (amour de soi) and compassion (pitie); inequality and conflict arise with society, private property and amour-propre, the desire for esteem in comparison with others. The Discourse notes that the first person who enclosed land and said "this is mine" was the founder of civil society.

The Social Contract (1762) begins "Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains" and asks how legitimate authority can be reconciled with freedom. The contract creates a form of association in which each, uniting with all, obeys only himself and remains as free as before. Key ideas:
- Freedom as obedience to a law one has prescribed oneself (moral freedom, autonomy).
- Sovereignty belongs to the people as a body and is inalienable and indivisible.
- The general will concerns the common good and differs from the "will of all", the sum of private interests.
- Those who refuse to obey the general will may be "forced to be free" (Book I, ch. 7).
- Representation cannot express sovereignty: the English people think they are free but are free only during the election of members of Parliament (Book III, ch. 15).
- Citizens need civic virtue, a modest equality of property, and sometimes a lawgiver and a civil religion.

Comparison
Both are contractarian, but Hobbes seeks peace through an absolute sovereign, with a negative view of liberty; Rousseau seeks a republic of self-ruling citizens, with a view of freedom as self-legislation. Rousseau's worry about inequality and dependence contrasts with Hobbes's focus on security.

Exam tips: be careful with the quotations and chapters; contrast the state of nature, the nature of sovereignty and the view of freedom.

Karl Marx and Friedrich Hayek offer opposed accounts of capitalism, freedom and the role of the state. Reading them together shows how contested the relation between markets and freedom is.

Marx
Historical materialism: In the 1859 Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, Marx argued that the economic base (forces and relations of production) shapes the legal, political and ideological superstructure. History is driven by conflicts between classes: in The Communist Manifesto (1848, with Engels) he says the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.

Alienation: In the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 (published in 1932), Marx argued that under capitalism workers are alienated from the product of their labour, from the activity of production, from their species-being (their creative potential) and from other people.

Exploitation: In Capital, volume I (1867), workers sell their labour power as a commodity and are paid its value (what is needed to reproduce it), yet in working they produce more value than they receive. The difference is surplus value, appropriated by the capitalist. Exploitation therefore does not depend on cheating in the exchange. Commodity fetishism describes how relations among people appear as relations among things.

State, rights and ideology: The Manifesto describes the executive of the modern state as a committee for managing the common affairs of the bourgeoisie. In "On the Jewish Question" (1843) Marx argues that political emancipation (equal rights and citizenship) is not human emancipation, as it leaves civil society, with its property and class divisions, intact. Ideology presents the ideas of the ruling class as universal (The German Ideology, written 1845-46).

Freedom: For Marx, wage-labour is a form of unfreedom: workers are compelled to sell their labour to survive. Real freedom is attained in communism, where production is collectively controlled and the "free development of each is the condition for the free development of all" (Manifesto). In the Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875) he sketched the principle "from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs". Critics argue that his account of the transition is thin, that planning has led to authoritarianism and that the labour theory of value is flawed.

Hayek
The Road to Serfdom (1944) argued that central economic planning leads to the concentration of power and the loss of political and individual freedom. In "The Use of Knowledge in Society" (American Economic Review, 1945), Hayek argued that the knowledge relevant for the economy is dispersed among countless individuals, much of it local and tacit, and cannot be gathered by a planner. The price system conveys this information and coordinates plans. In The Constitution of Liberty (1960) he defined freedom as the absence of coercion by the arbitrary will of another, and emphasised the rule of law: general, abstract and equal rules known in advance. In Law, Legislation and Liberty (1973-79) he defended spontaneous order and argued that "social justice" is a mirage, because market outcomes are not the result of anyone's intentions and cannot be called just or unjust. Hayek accepted a minimum safety net and some public goods, so he was not an anarchist or a minimal-state libertarian. Critics argue that he underestimates market power, that poverty restricts freedom, and that his rule-of-law argument allows too much inequality.

Contrast
Marx sees capitalist markets as a system of class domination; Hayek sees them as an impersonal order protecting individuals from the coercion of planners. Both concern the way impersonal systems shape agency.

Exam tips: do not conflate Hayek with Nozick; state each thinker's concept of freedom; and use Marx's exploitation point precisely.

notes.h: Overlooked voices: Macaulay, de Gouges, Douglass, Cooper, Nkrumah, Davis and the Combahee River Collective
notes.body:
The canon of political thought has often overlooked women, people of colour and thinkers from colonised regions, though they developed influential theories of freedom, equality, domination and resistance. This topic introduces several of them as political theorists in their own right.

Catharine Macaulay (1731-1791)
An English republican historian, Macaulay wrote the History of England (1763-83), which argued against Stuart absolutism. In Loose Remarks on Certain Positions to be found in Mr Hobbes's Philosophical Rudiments of Government and Society (1767) she criticised Hobbes and sketched a democratic form of government. In Observations on the Reflections of the Right Hon. Edmund Burke (1790) she answered Burke's defence of tradition, and her Letters on Education (1790) argued that the differences between men and women were largely a matter of education. She is a key figure of the republican tradition of freedom as independence from arbitrary power.

Olympe de Gouges (1748-1793)
A French writer and playwright, she wrote the Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen (1791), modelled on the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789). It argued that women are born free and equal in rights, that they have the right to political participation and, famously, that a woman has the right to mount the scaffold and so should also have the right to mount the rostrum. She also opposed slavery. She was executed in 1793 during the Terror.

Frederick Douglass (1818-1895)
Born into slavery in Maryland, he escaped in 1838 and became a leading abolitionist writer and orator. His Narrative (1845) described the dehumanising effects of slavery on both enslaved and enslavers. In "What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?" (delivered at Rochester, New York, on 5 July 1852) he told his audience that the day of national celebration highlighted the gap between American professions of liberty and the reality of slavery, which he regarded as proof of hypocrisy. In 1860 he argued, in a speech in Glasgow, that the US Constitution, properly interpreted, was an anti-slavery document, a position contested by William Lloyd Garrison.

Anna Julia Cooper (c. 1858-1964)
Born into slavery in North Carolina, Cooper became an educator and scholar. In A Voice from the South (1892) she argued that the position of women is a vital element in the progress of a people, and that Black women's education and standpoint were crucial: when Black women enter, the whole race enters with them. She argued for women's higher education and for a politics that attends to both race and gender, which anticipates intersectional analysis.

Kwame Nkrumah (1909-1972)
Leader of the Gold Coast independence movement, he became the colony's prime minister in 1952, led Ghana to independence in 1957 and became its first president in 1960. In Consciencism (1964) he set out a philosophy for decolonisation, and in Neo-Colonialism, the Last Stage of Imperialism (1965) he argued that a state may be formally independent while its economic system and political policy are directed from outside. He advocated Pan-African political union as a response.

Angela Davis (born 1944)
A philosopher and activist, Davis wrote Women, Race and Class (1981), which examined the tensions between the women's movement and the abolition and civil rights movements, and the experience of Black women. In Are Prisons Obsolete? (2003) she argued that the prison system perpetuates racialised punishment, tracing it to slavery, and advocated abolition.

The Combahee River Collective
A group of Black feminists in Boston, the Collective issued the Combahee River Collective Statement (1977), named after Harriet Tubman's 1863 raid on the Combahee River. It stated that racial, sexual, heterosexual and class oppression are interlocking, and that Black women's liberation requires analysing and fighting all of them together. It affirmed identity politics, arguing that the most profound politics comes from one's own identity, as opposed to working to end somebody else's oppression.

Exam tips: use primary texts and dates, link each thinker to a theme (freedom, domination, consent, oppression) and the canonical thinkers, and avoid treating these thinkers as only representatives of an identity.

The social contract presupposed an earlier sexual contract giving men authority over women, so contract theory conceals patriarchal power.
The social contract was also a racial contract treating non-white people as less than full persons; mainstream theory idealises away white supremacy.

Injustice produced by many people following accepted norms and rules, without a single dominator; developed in Responsibility for Justice (2011), building on Justice and the Politics of Difference (1990).
Overlapping systems such as race and sex create distinct disadvantage that single-axis analysis fails to capture.
A state formally independent whose economy and policy are directed from outside by foreign powers.
The global institutional order imposed by rich states contributes to severe poverty, so wealthy countries have duties of justice, not just charity.
Describing an inequality does not show it is unjust; an evaluative argument is needed, with premises about fairness, freedom or equality.
Absence of interference by others in the area within which a person could otherwise act. Answers 'How far does government interfere with me?'
Being one's own master and acting on one's own rational will; answers 'Who governs me?' Berlin feared it could justify coercion in the name of the 'real self'.
Rousseau's phrase (Social Contract, 1762): citizens who refuse the general will are compelled to follow it. Berlin saw this as a danger of positive liberty.
Freedom is a relation between an agent, a constraint and a goal: X is free from Y to do or become Z. Negative and positive stress different parts.
Pettit (1997): being free from the arbitrary power of another, even if never exercised; the slave with a kind master is unfree.
Liberty before Liberalism: freedom as independence from arbitrary power, drawn from Roman and Renaissance republican writers.
Sen (1999) and Nussbaum: freedom is what people are actually able to do and be, so material means and opportunities matter.
Power may rightfully be exercised over a person against their will only to prevent harm to others (On Liberty).
Political power is morally justified, so subjects have reason to obey, regardless of whether they believe it is; Weber's sense is descriptive (belief in legitimacy).
A threat that makes the person worse off than their baseline if they refuse, unlike an offer; the baseline is itself contested (Wertheimer 1987).
Leviathan ch. 14: covenants made out of fear in the state of nature are still obligatory; fear does not void a promise.
Second Treatise (1689, section 119): by using the benefits of a country, such as travelling on its highways, a person tacitly consents to its government.
'Of the Original Contract' (1748): residence is not consent, like a man carried aboard a ship while asleep who 'consents' by not jumping overboard.
Wolff (1970) and Simmons (1979): no state has a general moral authority over subjects, though particular commands may still be justified on other grounds.
Authority is legitimate if subjects better comply with the reasons that apply to them by following its directives than by acting on their own (The Morality of Freedom, 1986).
Those who benefit from a cooperative scheme owe their share of its burdens; Nozick objected that unrequested benefits cannot create obligations.
Citizens should be able to challenge and contest government decisions, so that public power is not arbitrary; elections alone are not enough.
Tocqueville (1835) and Madison (1787): democratic majorities may oppress minorities, which is why rights and institutional checks are needed.
Oppression is a network of interlocking barriers; examining a single wire cannot explain why the bird is trapped (The Politics of Reality).
Exploitation, marginalisation, powerlessness, cultural imperialism and violence (Justice and the Politics of Difference, 1990).
The dominant group's experience and culture are established as the norm, while the oppressed group is made invisible and marked as different (Young).
A speaker receives less credibility than deserved because of prejudice about their identity.
A gap in shared interpretive resources leaves someone unable to understand or communicate their experience, e.g. before 'sexual harassment' was named.
Pateman (1970) and Dahl (1985): participation in firms' decisions develops citizens and reduces employer domination.
Rawls's thought experiment: persons choose principles of justice behind a veil of ignorance about their class, talents, race, sex and conception of the good.
1. Equal basic liberties, with priority. 2. Fair equality of opportunity, and inequalities only if they benefit the least advantaged (difference principle).
Social and economic inequalities are justified only if they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society.
A distribution is just if it arose through just acquisition, just transfer and rectification of past injustice; justice is historical, not patterned.
Free exchanges upset any patterned distribution, so maintaining a pattern requires continuous interference with liberty (Nozick, 1974).
One may appropriate unowned things by mixing labour with them if 'enough, and as good' is left for others (Second Treatise, 1689).
Inequalities due to circumstances beyond a person's control are unjust, those due to choice are not (Dworkin 1981, Arneson, G. A. Cohen 1989).
Equality is about relations among equals, not cancelling luck; luck egalitarianism is demeaning and ignores oppression.
With no common power, roughly equal individuals fall into a war of all against all; life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' (Leviathan, ch. 13).
Competition (gain), diffidence (safety) and glory (reputation).
Each authorises a sovereign to act for all; sovereign authority is absolute and indivisible, but subjects keep the right of self-preservation.
Absence of external impediments to motion (ch. 21); liberty is the silence of the law. A negative conception.
Humans are driven by amour de soi (self-preservation) and pitie (compassion); inequality and conflict arise with society, property and amour-propre.

cards.f: General will vs will of all
cards.b: The general will aims at the common good; the will of all is the sum of private interests (Social Contract, 1762).
Social Contract, I.7: whoever refuses to obey the general will is compelled to do so by the whole body, which is not coercion of a free person but liberation.
Sovereignty cannot be represented; the English are free only during the election of members of Parliament (III.15).
The economic base (forces and relations of production) shapes the legal, political and ideological superstructure; history is driven by class conflict (1859 Preface).
Under capitalism the worker is alienated from the product, the productive activity, species-being and other people (1844 Manuscripts, published 1932).
Workers are paid the value of their labour power but produce more value; the surplus is appropriated by capitalists. No cheating in exchange is needed (Capital I, 1867).
Political emancipation (equal rights) is not human emancipation, since it leaves the class divisions of civil society intact.
Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875): the principle of distribution in the higher phase of communist society is 'to each according to his needs'.
'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945): economic knowledge is dispersed and tacit; prices coordinate it, which a central planner cannot replicate.
Constitution of Liberty (1960): freedom is the absence of coercion by the arbitrary will of another; the rule of law is its protection.
Law, Legislation and Liberty (1973-79): a 'mirage', since market outcomes are not produced by anyone's intention and so are neither just nor unjust.
Loose Remarks on Certain Positions to be found in Mr Hobbes's Philosophical Rudiments criticised Hobbes and sketched a democratic form of government.
Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen: women are born free and equal in rights and should have political participation. She was executed in 1793.

cards.f: Douglass, 'What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?' (1852)
cards.b: Delivered at Rochester on 5 July 1852: national celebrations of liberty highlight the contradiction with slavery, exposing hypocrisy.

cards.f: Cooper, A Voice from the South (1892)
cards.b: Black women's education and standpoint are central to progress; Cooper anticipated intersectional analysis of race and gender.
A state is formally independent and sovereign, but its economy and policy are directed from outside; Neo-Colonialism, the Last Stage of Imperialism.
Examines how the women's movement, abolition and civil rights intersected and conflicted, centring Black women's experience.
Are Prisons Obsolete? (2003): the prison system continues racialised punishment rooted in slavery; argues for abolition and alternatives.
Black feminist statement: racial, sexual, heterosexual and class oppression are interlocking, and Black women's liberation requires addressing all together.

questions.q: What is Anderson's central claim in Private Government (2017)?
options: Employment is a fully voluntary exchange among equals, so no power relation exists
Many workplaces involve unaccountable authority over workers that resembles government
Firms should be run directly by the state
Only state coercion can restrict freedom, not private employers
questions.why: Anderson argues that employers exercise extensive private authority that is hard to see because we focus on state power. The view that employment is purely voluntary among equals is the position she criticises. Saying only the state restricts freedom is the narrow view she challenges. She does not argue for state-run firms.

questions.q: What does 'intersectionality' (Crenshaw, 1989) highlight?
options: Overlapping systems such as race and sex can combine to create disadvantage that single-axis analysis misses
The largest form of oppression determines all others
Women's experiences are the same regardless of race
All forms of oppression have an identical structure
questions.why: Crenshaw showed that Black women could be excluded by analyses that treated race and sex separately. Claiming all oppression has an identical structure ignores differences she highlights. A single dominant form determining all others is a form of reductionism that intersectionality contests. The sameness of women's experiences across race is exactly the assumption she criticises.

questions.q: Explain what Young means by 'structural injustice' and how it differs from injustice caused by a wrongdoer.
markScheme: Structural injustice arises from many people acting within accepted rules and norms
No single perpetrator or intention required
Contrast: wrongdoing identifies a culpable agent
Responsibility is shared and forward-looking
Example: housing market or labour market disadvantage
questions.modelAnswer: Young (1990, 2011) argues that some injustices are structural: they result from the cumulative effect of many people pursuing their own goals within accepted rules and norms, such as in housing or labour markets, which together disadvantage certain groups. There is no single wrongdoer and no one need intend harm. By contrast, injustice by a wrongdoer involves an identifiable agent who breaks a rule and can be blamed and made to compensate. For structural injustice, Young argues that responsibility is shared: everyone who participates in the structures has a responsibility to work to change them, and responsibility is forward-looking rather than a matter of blame. This helps explain how inequalities in power can persist even when individuals act within the law and with no discriminatory intention.

questions.q: Which of these is Berlin's negative liberty?
options: Having the resources and capabilities needed to achieve one's goals
Self-mastery, acting in line with one's rational or higher self
Not being subject to the arbitrary power of others, even if it is not used
Absence of interference by others in the area in which a person could otherwise act
questions.why: Berlin defined negative liberty as non-interference. Self-mastery is his positive liberty. Freedom as security from arbitrary power, even unused, is the republican non-domination view of Pettit and Skinner. Having the means to achieve goals is the capability or 'worth of liberty' idea of Sen, Nussbaum and Rawls.

questions.q: On Pettit's republican account, a slave with a kind master who never interferes is:
options: free, as long as the master's rule is beneficial
partly free, in proportion to how kindly the master behaves
free, because freedom is only the absence of actual interference
unfree, because the master has the capacity to interfere arbitrarily
questions.why: For Pettit, domination is the capacity to interfere arbitrarily, so the slave is unfree whatever the master's kindness. The claim that freedom is only the absence of actual interference is the negative view that he argues against. Benefit to the slave or kindness is irrelevant because the slave's position still depends on the master's will. Kindness changes how the slave is treated, not whether the slave is dominated, so freedom does not come in degrees of kindness.

questions.q: Distinguish negative from positive liberty, and explain one danger Berlin associated with positive liberty.
markScheme: Negative: absence of interference
Positive: self-mastery, rational self-direction
Berlin's worry: 'real self' identified with reason or collective
Rulers may coerce people 'for their own good' ('forced to be free')
Brief reply: positive liberty includes legitimate autonomy; MacCallum's triadic account
questions.modelAnswer: Berlin (1958) distinguished negative liberty, the absence of interference by others in the sphere where a person could otherwise act, from positive liberty, the ideal of being one's own master and acting according to one's own rational purposes. His worry about the latter is that it can be distorted. If a person's true self is identified with reason or with the collective will, then authorities may claim to know what that self wants and coerce individuals in its name, so that freedom is turned into its opposite. He saw this danger in the idea, associated with Rousseau, that people can be forced to be free. Critics reply that autonomy is a valuable ideal that does not require such an interpretation, and that MacCallum's triadic view shows that the two concepts are different emphases within a single concept, so the danger depends on how it is interpreted rather than on positive liberty as such.

questions.q: Which example did Hume use to criticise the idea of tacit consent?
options: A person forced to be free by the general will
A traveller using the highway, who is said to consent by travelling
A man carried on board a ship while asleep, who is said to consent by not jumping overboard
A basketball player and the fans who pay to watch him
questions.why: Hume's ship example shows that remaining in a country need not be a free choice. The highway traveller is Locke's example of tacit consent, which Hume was criticising. The forced-to-be-free phrase is Rousseau's. The basketball player is Nozick's Wilt Chamberlain example in the debate about distributive justice.

questions.q: On Raz's service conception, an authority is legitimate if:
options: subjects would better comply with the reasons that apply to them by following its directives
its commands maximise total welfare
a majority of subjects accept its rule in elections
subjects have given express consent to its rule
questions.why: Raz's normal justification thesis says authority serves subjects by helping them conform to reasons. Express consent is the voluntarist position he rejects as too demanding. Welfare maximisation is a utilitarian test, not his. Majority acceptance is a procedural view of democratic legitimacy; for Raz, the point is the service the authority provides, not how many accept it.

questions.q: Evaluate tacit consent as a ground of political obligation.
markScheme: Locke: tacit consent through residence or use of benefits (section 119)
Hume's ship objection: no real choice, cannot leave
Consent should be voluntary and informed; exit costs high
Philosophical anarchism: Simmons
Alternatives: fairness, natural duty, hypothetical consent, service conception
questions.modelAnswer: Locke (Second Treatise, 1689, section 119) argued that anyone who enjoys the benefits of a country, even by travelling on its roads, tacitly consents to its government. This extends consent theory to people who have never expressly agreed. Hume (1748) objected that real consent must be voluntary and informed, and that most people live where they were born and cannot realistically leave, like someone carried onto a ship while asleep who is said to consent to the captain's authority by not jumping overboard. If consent is inferred from mere residence, it adds nothing to the fact of power. Simmons (1979) pressed the point, arguing that without real consent the state has no general authority, a position called philosophical anarchism. Defenders of consent might argue that the right to emigrate matters, but exit costs make this weak. Other accounts of obligation, such as fairness, natural duty and Raz's service conception, try to ground obedience without relying on consent, but each has its own objections. Tacit consent is therefore weak as a general ground of obligation.

questions.q: Which list gives Young's five faces of oppression?
options: The three dimensions of power: decisions, agenda-setting and preference shaping
Alienation from product, activity, species-being and other people
Exploitation, marginalisation, powerlessness, cultural imperialism and violence
Want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness
questions.why: Young's list is exploitation, marginalisation, powerlessness, cultural imperialism and violence. Want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness are Beveridge's five giants from his 1942 report. Alienation from product, activity, species-being and other people is Marx's analysis of alienated labour. The dimensions of decisions, agenda-setting and preference shaping are Lukes's three faces of power.

questions.q: What is Pettit's 'contestatory' conception of democracy?
options: Citizens must legislate directly rather than through representatives
Elected officials should be unconstrained because voters authorised them
Majority preferences aggregated at elections determine all policy
Citizens must be able to challenge government decisions, so public power is not arbitrary
questions.why: Pettit emphasises effective means of challenge and accountability alongside elections. Majority aggregation alone is the view that he treats as insufficient because it can leave minorities dominated. He does not require direct legislation. And unconstrained elected officials would be the situation of arbitrary power that republican theory seeks to avoid, even if the officials were elected.

questions.q: Explain Fricker's distinction between testimonial and hermeneutical injustice.
markScheme: Testimonial injustice: credibility deficit from prejudice
Hermeneutical injustice: gap in collective interpretive resources
Example of each
Link to oppression and power
Possible responses: epistemic virtues, inclusion
questions.modelAnswer: Fricker (2007) identifies two forms of epistemic injustice. Testimonial injustice occurs when prejudice causes a hearer to give a speaker's word less credibility than it deserves, for example when a person's account of a crime is disbelieved because of their race or gender. Hermeneutical injustice occurs when a gap in shared interpretive resources, caused by unequal social power in the making of concepts, leaves someone at an unfair disadvantage in making sense of their experience. The standard example is the experience of sexual harassment before the term existed, when victims struggled to describe or even to understand what was happening. The distinction shows that oppression can work through who is believed and which concepts are available, and not only through material or legal restrictions. Responses include cultivating epistemic virtues in hearers and making institutions and public discourse more inclusive.

questions.q: What does Rawls's difference principle require?
options: Inequalities are permissible if they result from voluntary transfers
Inequalities are permissible if they maximise total welfare
No inequalities of income or wealth are ever allowed
Inequalities are permissible only if they benefit the least advantaged members of society
questions.why: The difference principle justifies inequality only if it works to the benefit of the worst off. Banning all inequalities is stricter than Rawls, who accepts incentives that help the least advantaged. Allowing inequality that maximises total welfare is utilitarianism, which he rejected. Voluntary transfers as the test is Nozick's entitlement theory.

questions.q: What is the purpose of Nozick's Wilt Chamberlain example?
options: To show that markets produce just outcomes whatever the original holdings
To show that Rawls's difference principle would permit very high incomes
To show that free exchanges disturb any patterned distribution, so maintaining a pattern requires ongoing interference with liberty
To show that talented people deserve rewards in proportion to merit
questions.why: Nozick argues that even if a pattern is set up, voluntary transfers will upset it. He rejects desert as the basis of distribution, so the merit reading is wrong. Markets produce just outcomes only if holdings were justly acquired and transferred, with rectification, so the claim that they do whatever the original holdings is not his view. The example is not aimed at showing what the difference principle permits.

questions.q: Explain luck egalitarianism and one objection to it.
markScheme: Defines: inequalities from brute luck are unjust, those from choice are not
Dworkin (1981), Arneson, Cohen (1989)
Distinction between option luck and brute luck
Objection: Anderson (1999) relational equality; harsh to those who make poor choices
Other objections: difficulty of separating choice from circumstance
questions.modelAnswer: Luck egalitarianism holds that it is unfair for people to be worse off than others because of factors beyond their control, such as natural talents or social background, whereas inequalities arising from people's own choices can be just. Dworkin (1981) argued for equality of resources in which individuals are responsible for the costs of their choices but not for their circumstances, and Arneson and G. A. Cohen (1989) developed related views. It distinguishes brute luck from option luck, which is the result of deliberate gambles. Anderson (1999) objected that the view misconstrues the point of equality, which is to create a society of equals free from domination and oppression, not to compensate for bad luck. It would require the state to judge who is responsible for their situation, which is demeaning, and it might abandon those who made bad choices. A further objection is that choice and circumstance are hard to separate, since preferences themselves are shaped by circumstances.

questions.q: According to Hobbes, which is one of the three principal causes of quarrel in the state of nature?
options: Inequality of talents
Diffidence
Private property
Compassion
questions.why: Hobbes names competition, diffidence and glory. Private property as a source of conflict is Rousseau's view in the Discourse on Inequality. Compassion (pitie) is a natural sentiment for Rousseau, not a source of Hobbesian conflict. Hobbes in fact stresses natural equality: even the weakest can kill the strongest, so inequality of talents is not his cause of war.

questions.q: How does Rousseau distinguish the general will from the 'will of all'?
options: The general will is expressed by representatives, while the will of all is expressed directly
The general will is the sovereign's command, while the will of all is the subjects' obedience
The general will is whatever a majority votes for, while the will of all is what the elite wants
The general will aims at the common good, while the will of all is the sum of private wills
questions.why: For Rousseau the general will concerns the common good and can differ from what everyone wants as private individuals. A majority vote may or may not track the general will, so defining it as a majority vote is wrong. Rousseau denies that the general will can be represented, so the claim that it is expressed by representatives reverses his view. Treating the general will as the sovereign's command and the will of all as the subjects' obedience mixes up roles; for Rousseau the people are both sovereign and subjects.

questions.q: Compare Hobbes's and Rousseau's accounts of the state of nature and their implications for political authority.
markScheme: Hobbes: war of all against all; fear, competition, glory
Rousseau: natural goodness; corruption by society, property, amour-propre
Hobbes: absolute sovereign for security
Rousseau: popular sovereignty and general will; freedom as autonomy
Evaluation or key contrast: negative vs positive liberty; danger of each
questions.modelAnswer: For Hobbes (1651), the state of nature, a condition without common power, is a war of all against all driven by competition, diffidence and glory. Life is insecure, so individuals rationally authorise a sovereign with absolute power to secure peace. Authority is justified by its ability to protect, and subjects keep only the right to self-preservation. Liberty is the absence of impediments, which law leaves untouched. Rousseau (1755, 1762) argued that Hobbes read the characteristics of society back into nature. For him natural humans are not warlike; inequality, dependence and conflict come from private property and amour-propre. The solution is not submission but a contract creating a political community in which sovereignty belongs to the people and laws express the general will. Freedom is obedience to self-prescribed law. The contrast shows two models of legitimacy: security-based authority with a negative view of liberty, and self-rule with a more positive one. Each carries risks: Hobbes' sovereign may be tyrannical, and Rousseau's general will may justify coercion of dissenters.

questions.q: What is Hayek's main point in 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945)?
options: Economic knowledge is dispersed among individuals, and prices coordinate it in a way a central planner cannot
Prices reflect the labour time embodied in goods
Markets inevitably lead to monopoly
A planner with enough data can aggregate all economic knowledge
questions.why: Hayek's knowledge problem says the relevant information is local and tacit, so central planning cannot succeed. The idea that a planner can aggregate everything is the assumption Hayek criticises. Inevitable monopoly is a Marxist-inspired claim rather than Hayek's. The labour theory of value belongs to classical economics and Marx, and Hayek's price argument is about information, not labour content.

questions.q: On Marx's account in Capital, exploitation occurs because:
options: employers pay workers less than the going market wage
the state taxes wages at a higher rate than profits
workers produce more value than the value of their wages, and the surplus is kept by capitalists, even when exchanges are fair
employers regularly break the contracts they agree with workers
questions.why: Marx argued that labour power is bought at its value, yet it produces more value than it costs, so exploitation exists even without cheating in the exchange. Underpaying relative to the market wage describes ordinary wage theft or monopsony, which is a different complaint. Breach of contract is not needed for his argument. Taxation is not part of his explanation of exploitation.

questions.q: Contrast Marx's and Hayek's views of freedom in a market society.
markScheme: Marx: wage-labour as unfreedom; alienation, exploitation; freedom through collective control
Hayek: freedom as absence of coercion; market as impersonal order; rule of law
Hayek's knowledge argument against planning
Marx's critique of formal rights; Hayek's critique of 'social justice'
Evaluation: both address impersonal systems; each has blind spots
questions.modelAnswer: Marx argues that in capitalist society workers are formally free to contract but compelled by economic necessity to sell their labour, which is alienating and exploitative; the capitalist appropriates surplus value, so freedom is limited to formal rights while real power lies with capital. Real freedom would require collective control of production and the end of class domination. Hayek (1960) defines freedom as the absence of coercion by the arbitrary will of another, protected by general rules under the rule of law. For him markets are an impersonal order in which no person commands another, and central planning is dangerous because it concentrates power and, as he argued in 1945, cannot use dispersed knowledge. He rejects the idea of social justice as applied to market outcomes. The two disagree on whether economic dependence is coercion: Marx says it is a form of structural domination, Hayek that poverty or dependence is not coercion unless someone deliberately imposes it. Hayek's view may neglect market power, while Marx's alternative faces the knowledge and authoritarianism objections.

questions.q: What is the main claim of the Combahee River Collective Statement (1977)?
options: Black women should avoid coalition politics altogether
Class oppression alone explains Black women's situation, so race and sex are secondary
Feminism should focus on the concerns of white middle-class women to build a wider coalition
Racial, sexual, heterosexual and class oppression are interlocking, so Black women's liberation requires analysing them together
questions.why: The Statement stresses interlocking oppressions. Treating class as the sole explanation is the orthodox Marxist view that it criticises. Focusing on white middle-class women's concerns is the feminist tendency it challenges. It does not reject all coalition politics; it supports coalition on appropriate terms while grounding politics in Black women's own identity.

questions.q: How did Nkrumah define 'neo-colonialism' in 1965?
options: A Pan-African political union of African states
Direct administrative rule of a territory by a colonial power
A formally independent state whose economic system and political policy are directed from outside
The constitutional transfer of power at independence
questions.why: Nkrumah's neo-colonialism is control without formal rule. Direct administrative rule is classical colonialism, the thing neo-colonialism supposedly replaces. A constitutional transfer of power describes decolonisation itself, which he argued did not necessarily end external control. Pan-African union was his proposed remedy, not the definition of the problem.

questions.q: How does Douglass's 'What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?' (1852) challenge American ideas of liberty?
markScheme: Context: delivered at Rochester, 5 July 1852
Contrast between professed ideals and slavery
Charge of national hypocrisy
Uses founders' own principles as a standard
Link to wider argument about the Constitution or about freedom/domination
questions.modelAnswer: Douglass delivered the speech at Rochester, New York, on 5 July 1852. Addressing a white audience celebrating independence, he asked what the holiday meant to enslaved people and answered that it revealed the distance between the nation's professed principles of liberty and equality and its practice of slavery. He distanced himself from the celebration, noting that the inheritance of liberty and justice his audience celebrated was not shared by the enslaved. He charged the nation with hypocrisy while appealing to the founders' ideals as a standard by which slavery stood condemned. The speech therefore challenges American self-understanding by showing that liberty for some depended on the domination of others, and it connects with the republican view of freedom as non-domination, since slavery is the paradigm of unfreedom. In 1860 Douglass argued that a proper reading of the Constitution was anti-slavery, which indicates he took the founding principles seriously as ideals.

questions.q: Is freedom better understood as non-interference or as non-domination?
markScheme: Defines negative liberty (Berlin 1958) and non-domination (Pettit 1997, Skinner 1998)
Applies to cases: slave with kind master, workplace (Anderson 2017)
Arguments for non-interference: clarity, protection against paternalism, Berlin's warning
Arguments for non-domination: captures dependence on arbitrary power; compatible with law not reducing freedom
Objections to non-domination (Carter, Kramer, Berlin-style): vagueness of 'arbitrary', moralised concept; to non-interference: ignores dependence
Possible reconciliation: MacCallum, or different roles of the concepts
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer: Berlin (1958) defined negative liberty as the absence of interference by others in the area in which a person could otherwise act, and warned that positive liberty could be abused. Republicans such as Pettit (1997) and Skinner (1998) argue that this misses what matters: being subject to the arbitrary power of another, even if it is not used. The slave with a kind master illustrates the contrast. On the negative view, the slave is free to the extent that the master does not interfere; on the republican view, the slave is unfree because the master can interfere at will, and so the slave must act with the master's favour in mind. Similar reasoning applies to employees who depend on an employer with wide powers (Anderson, 2017), to spouses who are economically dependent, and to citizens subject to an unaccountable government. Non-domination also explains why laws are not necessarily an infringement of freedom: laws that citizens can control and contest are non-arbitrary. There are reasons to prefer the negative conception. Carter (1999) and Kramer argue that the republican concept is moralised: to judge whether power is arbitrary, we need a theory of what interference is justified, so the concept of freedom is no longer descriptive, and they say that republicans misclassify the kind master: it is better to say the slave is free in many respects but insecure. Negative liberty is also clearer and easier to measure, and it protects individuals from paternalism by authorities that claim to know their real interests. On the other hand, a focus on interference neglects the effects of dependence on choices (the slave will anticipate and self-censor), and it implies that a benevolent dictator who rarely interferes secures a high degree of freedom. These two views can be partly reconciled: MacCallum's triadic analysis shows that they emphasise different parts of the same relation, and one can distinguish freedom as the absence of interference from the security or status of non-domination. My conclusion is that non-domination better captures the value that makes freedom important in political life, namely independence from the will of others, but it needs a more precise account of arbitrariness, and the negative concept remains useful in analysing particular constraints.

questions.q: Which poses the greater threat to freedom: the state or the market? Discuss with reference to Hobbes, Rousseau, Marx and Hayek.
markScheme: Frames the question and defines freedom for each thinker
Hobbes: state as protector; sovereign's power; liberty as absence of impediment
Rousseau: dependence, inequality; general will; risk of coercion
Marx: wage labour as unfreedom; alienation; state as class instrument
Hayek: planning/state coercion; market as impersonal order
Weighs: state coercion vs structural domination; role of rule of law and democratic control
Reasoned conclusion that avoids false dichotomy
questions.modelAnswer: The question depends on what freedom means. Hobbes (1651) defines liberty as the absence of external impediments and argues that the greatest threat to freedom is the insecurity of the state of nature; an absolute sovereign is justified because it protects life. For him the main threat to freedom is the absence of the state, though he recognises the sovereign's power is great. Rousseau (1762) agrees that order requires a state, but sees threats to freedom in dependence on other people created by inequality and private property. Freedom is obeying a law one has made oneself, so the danger is both a state not based on the general will, and market society which creates dependence and amour-propre. Yet his idea of forcing people to be free reveals the possible threat from a state that claims to speak for the general will. Marx (1867) argues that capitalism compels workers to sell their labour, alienating and exploiting them; the market is a structure of class domination, and the state is a committee of the bourgeoisie. So the market threatens freedom directly, and the state serves it until a transformation of property relations. Hayek (1944, 1960) takes the opposite view: the market is an impersonal order in which no one commands another, and the main threat comes from planners and legislators who concentrate power and use coercion; knowledge is dispersed, so central planning cannot succeed without compulsion. Assessing these views, the dichotomy is partly false. Hayek is right that concentrated state power is dangerous, and twentieth-century planned economies support the worry; but his definition of coercion as deliberate interference may ignore the effect of economic dependence which Marx and Rousseau emphasise, and Hayek himself accepts a safety net. Marx's point that wage dependence limits real choice is strong, but his account of the alternative does not explain how to prevent a new concentration of power. A republican view such as that developed by Pettit offers a way of combining them: both state and market can be sources of arbitrary power, and freedom requires that power in both be subject to law and to contestation by those affected. In conclusion, neither is inherently the greater threat; the danger comes from unaccountable power wherever it arises, and the task is to institutionalise accountability in both the state and the economy.
